lines.text: Pray thee, sweet Mistress Margaret, deserve well at my hands by helping me to the speech of Beatrice.
lines.plainText: Pray thee sweet Mistress Margaret deserve well at my hands by helping me to the speech of Beatrice

lines.text: Will you then write me a sonnet in praise of my beauty?
lines.plainText: Will you then write me a sonnet in praise of my beauty

lines.text: In so high a style, Margaret, that no man living shall come over it; for, in most comely truth, thou deservest it.
lines.plainText: In so high a style Margaret that no man living shall come over it for in most comely truth thou deservest it

lines.text: To have no man come over me! why, shall I always keep below stairs?
lines.plainText: To have no man come over me why shall I always keep below stairs

lines.text: Thy wit is as quick as the greyhound's mouth; it catches.
lines.plainText: Thy wit is as quick as the greyhound's mouth it catches

lines.text: And yours as blunt as the fencer's foils, which hit, but hurt not.
lines.plainText: And yours as blunt as the fencer's foils which hit but hurt not

lines.text: A most manly wit, Margaret; it will not hurt a woman: and so, I pray thee, call Beatrice. I give thee the bucklers.
lines.plainText: A most manly wit Margaret it will not hurt a woman and so I pray thee call Beatrice I give thee the bucklers

lines.text: Give us the swords, we have bucklers of our own.
lines.plainText: Give us the swords we have bucklers of our own

lines.text: If you use them, Margaret, you must put in the pikes with a vice; and they are dangerous weapons for maids.
lines.plainText: If you use them Margaret you must put in the pikes with a vice and they are dangerous weapons for maids

lines.text: Well, I will call Beatrice to you, who I think hath legs.
lines.plainText: Well I will call Beatrice to you who I think hath legs

lines.text: And therefore will come.
lines.plainText: And therefore will come

lines.text: Yea, signior; and depart when you bid me.
lines.plainText: Yea signior and depart when you bid me

lines.text: O, stay but till then!
lines.plainText: O stay but till then

lines.text: 'Then' is spoken; fare you well now: and yet, ere I go, let me go with that I came for; which is, with knowing what hath passed between you and Claudio.
lines.plainText: 'Then' is spoken fare you well now and yet ere I go let me go with that I came for which is with knowing what hath passed between you and Claudio

lines.text: Only foul words; and thereupon I will kiss thee.
lines.plainText: Only foul words and thereupon I will kiss thee

lines.text: Foul words is but foul wind, and foul wind is but foul breath, and foul breath is noisome; therefore I will depart unkissed.
lines.plainText: Foul words is but foul wind and foul wind is but foul breath and foul breath is noisome therefore I will depart unkissed

lines.text: Thou hast frighted the word out of his right sense, so forcible is thy wit. But I must tell thee plainly, Claudio undergoes my challenge, and either I must shortly hear from him, or I will subscribe him a coward. And, I pray thee now, tell me, for which of my bad parts didst thou first fall in love with me?
lines.plainText: Thou hast frighted the word out of his right sense so forcible is thy wit But I must tell thee plainly Claudio undergoes my challenge and either I must shortly hear from him or I will subscribe him a coward And I pray thee now tell me for which of my bad parts didst thou first fall in love with me

lines.text: For them all together; which maintained so politic a state of evil that they will not admit any good part to intermingle with them. But for which of my good parts did you first suffer love for me?
lines.plainText: For them all together which maintained so politic a state of evil that they will not admit any good part to intermingle with them But for which of my good parts did you first suffer love for me

lines.text: 'Suffer love,' a good epithet! I do suffer love indeed, for I love thee against my will.
lines.plainText: 'Suffer love' a good epithet I do suffer love indeed for I love thee against my will

lines.text: In spite of your heart, I think. Alas, poor heart! If you spite it for my sake, I will spite it for yours; for I will never love that which my friend hates.
lines.plainText: In spite of your heart I think Alas poor heart If you spite it for my sake I will spite it for yours for I will never love that which my friend hates

lines.text: Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably.
lines.plainText: Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably

lines.text: It appears not in this confession: there's not one wise man among twenty that will praise himself.
lines.plainText: It appears not in this confession there's not one wise man among twenty that will praise himself

lines.text: An old, an old instance, Beatrice, that lived in the time of good neighbours. If a man do not erect in this age his own tomb ere he dies, he shall live no longer in monument than the bell rings and the widow weeps.
lines.plainText: An old an old instance Beatrice that lived in the time of good neighbours If a man do not erect in this age his own tomb ere he dies he shall live no longer in monument than the bell rings and the widow weeps

lines.text: And how long is that think you?
lines.plainText: And how long is that think you

lines.text: Question: why, an hour in clamour and a quarter in rheum: therefore is it most expedient for the wise,—if Don Worm, his conscience, find no impediment to the contrary,—to be the trumpet of his own virtues, as I am to myself. So much for praising myself, who, I myself will bear witness, is praiseworthy. And now tell me, how doth your cousin?
lines.plainText: Question why an hour in clamour and a quarter in rheum therefore is it most expedient for the wiseif Don Worm his conscience find no impediment to the contraryto be the trumpet of his own virtues as I am to myself So much for praising myself who I myself will bear witness is praiseworthy And now tell me how doth your cousin

lines.text: Very ill.
lines.plainText: Very ill

lines.text: And how do you?
lines.plainText: And how do you

lines.text: Very ill too.
lines.plainText: Very ill too

lines.text: Serve God, love me, and mend. There will I leave you too, for here comes one in haste.
lines.plainText: Serve God love me and mend There will I leave you too for here comes one in haste

lines.text: Madam, you must come to your uncle. Yonder's old coil at home: it is proved, my Lady Hero hath been falsely accused, the Prince and Claudio mightily abused; and Don John is the author of all, who is fled and gone. Will you come presently?
lines.plainText: Madam you must come to your uncle Yonder's old coil at home it is proved my Lady Hero hath been falsely accused the Prince and Claudio mightily abused and Don John is the author of all who is fled and gone Will you come presently

lines.text: Will you go hear this news, signior?
lines.plainText: Will you go hear this news signior

lines.text: I will live in thy heart, die in thy lap, and be buried in thy eyes; and moreover I will go with thee to thy uncle's.
lines.plainText: I will live in thy heart die in thy lap and be buried in thy eyes and moreover I will go with thee to thy uncle's
